raw_response:
I found four useful candidates or workflows, but the evidence does not establish a single tool that met every requirement on 8 January 2020. The pages inspected are live, undated documentation. Their feature descriptions should not be treated as proof of availability at that cutoff.

**1. SoapUI Open Source — the GUI candidate to investigate first.** SoapUI organizes work into projects and saves each project, including its tests and scripts, as an XML file suitable for version control. Its bundled command-line runner can select a test suite or test case. These are strong matches for separate logical groupings, portable files, and selective execution. However, the Swagger/OpenAPI documentation lists version 2.0 support; it does not establish OAS 3 support. The import section I read specifies a local definition file, so direct import from an arbitrary OpenAPI URL remains unverified. Imported REST services also need test suites to be added. Some runner options are explicitly restricted to ReadyAPI, although the basic runner is included. Sources: [Swagger/OpenAPI support](https://www.soapui.org/docs/rest-testing/openapi-swagger-support/), [project organization and files](https://www.soapui.org/docs/getting-started/projects/working-with-projects/), and [command-line execution](https://www.soapui.org/docs/automation/running-functional-tests/).

**2. OpenAPI-to-Postman plus Newman — a collection-file workflow.** The converter takes an OpenAPI specification file and writes a Postman collection file; Newman runs collections and can select folders or individual requests. Separate collection files and directories can provide the logical groupings and Git workflow you want. Fetching a remote specification before conversion is an additional step: the converter's documented CLI source argument is a file path. This gives a practical CLI-oriented mechanism, but not a replacement graphical workspace editor, and I did not separately verify licensing terms or historical feature versions. Sources: [converter documentation](https://github.com/postmanlabs/openapi-to-postman/blob/develop/README.md) and [Newman](https://github.com/postmanlabs/newman).

**3. Portman — a more integrated OpenAPI-to-collection route.** Its documented CLI accepts a remotely hosted specification, writes a local Postman collection, and can invoke Newman. Its operation filters and generated integration-test folders can help define selected groups of requests. That directly addresses the specification-URL requirement better than the converter's local-file CLI. Multiple configurations and output files could serve as separate workspaces; that is a proposed way to apply the tool, not a verified GUI workspace feature. This is an automation-oriented candidate, and I have not established its availability by the question date or independently checked its licensing. Source: [Portman README and CLI examples](https://github.com/apideck-libraries/portman/blob/main/README.md?plain=1).

**4. Noodle — a terminal client with collections stored beside code.** The current README describes free, Apache-licensed software with YAML request files, folders, OpenAPI/Swagger import, Postman export, and a CLI collection runner supporting request and folder selection. This is a promising fit if a terminal interface is acceptable. Direct OpenAPI URL input was not established by the page inspected, and the documented current features have no verified connection to the 2020 cutoff. Source: [Noodle](https://github.com/noodle-rest/noodle).

For a GUI workflow, I would first test SoapUI against the actual specification, especially its OpenAPI version. For a CLI workflow, Portman's URL-to-collection path or the converter-plus-Newman combination are useful starting points. Noodle is another filesystem-oriented option to assess against the URL requirement. I would not describe any of these as an unconditional match until those remaining gaps are resolved.

The discovery included broad client searches, targeted SoapUI and Advanced REST Client searches, and a collection-generation alternative. Advanced REST Client's documentation confirmed its free-tool philosophy, but the inspected evidence did not establish the required command-line execution or Postman export, so it is not included as a candidate. The unauthenticated grep.app endpoint was inaccessible; the code-related evidence above came through web-indexed public GitHub material, not a successful native code-search result.
